openers.stenian-period: The Stenian is the period of sex, failed rifts and growing supercontinents. Bangiomorpha, a red alga from Arctic Canada, carries the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction, and the earliest known fungus appears in shale nearby. In the middle of North America, the crust began to split along a rift 2,000 km long, then stopped. Mountain building in Scandinavia and the Grand Canyon's first layers record a world assembling Rodinia, while an impact in Scotland left its debris but no crater anyone has found.
openers.neoproterozoic-era: The Neoproterozoic is the era in which life began to get big. Eukaryotes, long inconspicuous, diversified rapidly around 1 billion years ago, green algae became multicellular, and sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 million years old may be the oldest animals. A second great rise in oxygen swept the air and oceans. Meanwhile Rodinia began to rift apart, island arcs built the Arabian-Nubian Shield, and the pieces of a new southern continent, Gondwana, started to come together.
openers.tonian-period: The Tonian is when eukaryotes finally stepped forward. They diversified rapidly around 1 billion years ago, dominated fresh water in Scotland's Torridon lakes, and by about 800 million years ago left fossils notably more complex and numerous. Oxygen began its second great rise, and the first possible animals appear as sponge-like fossils. Under it all, the supercontinent Rodinia started to break apart, opening new oceans as old ones closed.

reviews.ectasian-period: The Ectasian links one supercontinent's end to another's beginning. A superplume and great igneous provinces, from the 1,380-million-year-old event to the Mackenzie floods, split Columbia apart. Its fragments then collided again in the Kibaran, Grenville and Musgrave orogenies to build Rodinia, with Laurentia at its core. In the shallow seas stromatolites reached their peak, just before grazing life began to push them into a long decline.
reviews.stenian-period: The Stenian shows Rodinia's assembly and life's growing sophistication side by side. Collisions such as the Sveconorwegian thickened crust while the Midcontinent Rift tried and failed to split North America, its lavas now lying beneath Lake Superior. In lakes and seas, life grew more complex: Bangiomorpha left the oldest evidence of sex, Ourasphaira the earliest known fungus, and the Nonesuch and Lakhanda rocks preserved whole microbial communities. Sex in particular sped up evolution, setting up the eukaryote boom to come.
reviews.tonian-period: The Tonian ties a breaking supercontinent to a blossoming of life. As Rodinia rifted, oceans like the Pharusian opened and Gondwana began to assemble through the East African Orogeny. At the same time, a second rise in oxygen and falling sulfide in the seas let eukaryotes diversify, colonize fresh water and grow armor against new predators, while planktonic cyanobacteria spread offshore. The first possible animals, sponge-like fossils, appeared, and the breakup itself may have triggered the Cryogenian ice that followed.

prot-071.title: Rodinia assembles
prot-071.text:
The broken pieces of one supercontinent came back together as another. Fragments of Columbia, scattered by {{ref:prot-063}}, accreted and collided to form Rodinia, which assembled between 1.26 and 0.90 billion years ago.

Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, sat at its center. Around it, Rodinia grew into the largest landmass yet, joining North American, East European, Amazonian, West African, Antarctic, Australian and Chinese blocks. Baltica and Amazonia collided with Laurentia in the Grenville, Sveconorwegian and Sunsás orogenies, between 1.1 and 0.9 billion years ago.

A single global ocean, Mirovia, surrounded it. Later, the proto-Pacific Panthalassa grew at Mirovia's expense.

For all its size, Rodinia remains shadowy. Its configuration and history are much less well understood than those of later supercontinents, because its rocks are older, more deformed and more scattered. Even so, its later breakup would reshape the climate and help set the scene for animal life.

prot-073.title: Stromatolites peak, then fall
prot-073.text:
For most of Earth's history, the most visible life was a mound of slime and sediment. Stromatolites, mounds built by microbial colonies, reached their greatest abundance and diversity about 1.25 billion years ago. Widespread colonies and reefs of cyanobacteria then dominated the tidal zones of oceans and seas.

After that, they declined steeply, perhaps as predators began grazing on stromatolites and acritarchs. The decline sped up around 1 billion years ago, at the end of the Stenian, and grazing by more complex organisms is the most widely supported explanation. By the start of the Cambrian they had fallen to 20% of their peak.

prot-072.title: The Grenville orogeny
prot-072.text:
The roots of the Appalachian Mountains go back more than a billion years. A long-lived mountain-building event, tied to the assembly of Rodinia, raised a belt from Labrador to Mexico and on to Scotland. Laurentia collided with other blocks, notably Amazonia, beginning the construction of what are now the Appalachians.

Its main pulses were the Elzevirian (1240–1220 million years ago), Ottawan (1090–1020 million) and Rigolet (1010–980 million). From about 1190 to 980 million years ago, two continental blocks collided with Laurentia, folding mountains from Newfoundland to North Carolina. Crust of this age turns up worldwide, where the same events are called Kibaran in Africa, Dalslandian in western Europe and Sunsás in Brazil.

prot-074.title: The Musgrave orogeny in central Australia
prot-074.text: In the red center of Australia, a magma plume built a region of 220,000 km². This Musgrave Province was shaped by three orogenic events between 1.22 and 1.12 billion years ago. The Musgravian orogeny, about 1,200 million years ago, melted the lower crust and generated the voluminous Kulgera granites. The province is one of the many belts of crust formed or reworked as Rodinia came together.

prot-077.title: The Stac Fada impact and its missing crater
prot-077.text: Somewhere in Scotland lies a crater nobody has found. The Stac Fada Member, a layer of rock in the northwest Highlands, records an impact about 1.2 billion years ago. From its debris, geologists infer a crater about 40 km wide. That crater has not been found, and it may lie hidden beneath younger rock or have been worn away.

prot-075.title: The Grand Canyon Supergroup
prot-075.text: Halfway down the Grand Canyon, tilted layers record half a billion years of seafloor. Nine formations of the Grand Canyon Supergroup were laid down in a sea between 1.2 billion and 740 million years ago, the Chuar Group in coastal and shallow seas. Its oldest layer, averaging 1250 million years, is the oldest in the canyon with fossils, stromatolites. The Cardenas Basalt, 1070 ± 70 million years old, tops the Unkar Group. About 800 million years ago the Grand Canyon orogeny tilted the supergroup 15° and broke it into fault blocks.

prot-078.title: The Sveconorwegian orogeny
prot-078.text: Southern Norway and southwestern Sweden were remade during Rodinia's assembly. A mountain-building system was active there from 1140 to 960 million years ago. Its most active phase, 1050–980 million years ago, metamorphosed and thickened the crust. A collision between Amazonia and Baltica may have caused it. It is grouped with the Grenvillian orogens, such as {{ref:prot-072}}, that assembled Rodinia.

prot-080.title: The Midcontinent Rift, a split that failed
prot-080.text:
Lake Superior fills the valley of a rift that almost tore North America in two. About 1.1 billion years ago, the continent's core began to split apart, opening a rift 2,000 km long through its middle. Lava poured from cracks along the rift valley. Its arms meet at Lake Superior. The western arm runs through Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Nebraska, and the eastern arm reaches central Michigan.

Then the rift failed. It left thick layers of igneous rock and became the deepest failed rift on Earth. Magmatism of about the same age struck Africa, India and South America.

prot-082.title: The Nonesuch lake fossils
prot-082.text: A billion-year-old lake in Michigan held enough oxygen to keep its microbes in fine detail. The lake lay in the Midcontinent Rift, and its exceptionally preserved freshwater microbes make it a Lagerstätte, a site of unusually good fossils. Its shale, siltstone and sandstone, 150–210 m thick, extend from Michigan and Wisconsin to Iowa. It offers a rare look at life in fresh water, far from the sea.

prot-083.title: The Warakurna large igneous province
prot-083.text: Central Australia was flooded with magma about 1.08 billion years ago. The Warakurna large igneous province intruded the Giles Complex and Winburn granites and erupted the volcanic rocks of the Bentley Supergroup. Some have looked for a link to a 1110-million-year-old event in Africa, India and Amazonia. A link is possible but unlikely, so Warakurna appears to stand as its own event.

prot-084.title: Bangiomorpha, the first known sexual organism
prot-084.text:
The oldest evidence of sex comes from a tiny red seaweed in the Canadian Arctic. Bangiomorpha pubescens, a multicellular red alga from Somerset Island, closely resembles the living red alga Bangia, about 1.05 billion years later.

Its differentiated reproductive cells are the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction and of meiosis, the cell division that makes sex cells with half the usual set of genes. It is also the earliest known organism that certainly had differentiated, specialized cells. And it is the oldest belonging to a living phylum, one of the major branches of life.

Why does it matter? Sex mixes the genes of two parents, so it increased genetic variation. That variation sped up evolution and the diversification of eukaryotes. The boom described in {{ref:prot-087}} may owe something to this small alga.

prot-085.title: The Lakhanda Group fossils
prot-085.text: Even a billion years ago, microbes were eating each other. The Lakhanda Group of Russia's Uchur-Maya Depression preserves a community dominated by anaerobic bacteria, microbes that live without oxygen. The fossils also show evidence of food-web interactions, organisms feeding on other organisms. That makes the site a Lagerstätte, an unusually rich fossil bed, and an early glimpse of an ecosystem with links between its members.

prot-086.title: Ourasphaira, the earliest known fungus
prot-086.text: Mushrooms have a very long pedigree. Shale of the Grassy Bay Formation, in the Canadian Arctic, preserves Ourasphaira giraldae, multicellular organic-walled microfossils with fungal affinity. Dated to 1.01–0.89 billion years, it is the earliest known fungus. Older fossils, from 1.43 billion years ago, have also been interpreted as multicellular fungi with differentiated cells, so the group may be older still.

prot-087.title: Eukaryotes diversify as acritarchs boom
prot-087.text:
After a long, quiet career, eukaryotes suddenly bloomed. Around 1 billion years ago they diversified rapidly. Acritarchs, organic-walled microfossils, boomed in abundance, diversity, size and shape in their first large radiation, growing more and longer spines.

The spines may have been armor. The first dinoflagellates, some of which ate prey, may have been the first predators, pushing acritarchs into an arms race of defenses. Life got faster too. After 1 billion years ago, species lasted only about 100 million years, perhaps because early protists, single-celled eukaryotes, grazed more heavily.

prot-088.title: Eukaryotes take over fresh water
prot-088.text:
Lakes and rivers belonged to complex cells by a billion years ago. Abundant eukaryotic microfossils from Scotland's freshwater Torridon Group suggest eukaryotes dominated non-marine habitats by then, including multicellular forms. Nutrients from continental runoff probably favored them near the continents.

Phosphatic microfossils from Scotland's Diabaig Formation, 994 ± 48 million years old, are among the oldest known non-marine eukaryotes. Molecular-clock evidence goes further. It suggests that photosynthetic, multicellular eukaryotes and fungi had moved onto land by 1000 million years ago.

prot-089.title: Proterocladus, the first multicellular green alga
prot-089.text:
Every land plant descends from green algae, and the oldest many-celled one is about 1 billion years old. Proterocladus antiquus is the first known preserved case of multicellularity in green algae. Around this time, the first multicellular plants emerged, probably green algae.

Where a colony of cells ends and a true multicellular organism begins is blurred. Still, Proterocladus shows green algae building bodies of many cells. They joined the red algae of {{ref:prot-084}} among the first seaweeds.

prot-090.title: The late Ruker orogeny under Antarctic ice
prot-090.text: Antarctica hides a mountain range beneath its ice, and it may be a billion years old. Around 1 billion years ago, a mountain-building event, also called the Nimrod orogeny, struck the continent. It may have begun the Gamburtsev mountain range and the Vostok Subglacial Highlands, both now buried under the ice sheet. Its date is uncertain by about 150 million years.

prot-091.title: The Rayner orogeny joins India and Antarctica
prot-091.text: Part of Antarctica is a continuation of India. Proto-India and Antarctica collided in the Rayner orogeny, from about 1,000 million years ago until about 900 million. Rocks of East Antarctica's Rayner Complex and northern Prince Charles Mountains are an extension of India's Eastern Ghats. They belong to a Grenville-age belt along East Antarctica's coast, read as a suture with southern Africa, India and western Australia.

prot-093.title: Bitter Springs microfossils
prot-093.text: Some fossils are so well preserved that their insides still show. Cherts of Australia's Bitter Springs Group preserve stromatolites and exceptionally well-preserved cyanobacteria in silica. Some fossils with ghostly internal structures, such as Glenobotrydion, have been read as green algae, among the earliest plants, though that claim is debated. This style of preservation ended in the late Neoproterozoic, when organisms that secrete silica appeared and took it from the water.

prot-094.title: The first possible animals
prot-094.text:
The animal kingdom may have begun as something like a sponge on a reef. Sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 million years old may be the oldest animals, but their identity is highly debated. The first putative animal fossils date to the middle to late Tonian, about 890–800 million years ago. Otavia, about 800 million years old, has been described as a primitive sponge.

Molecular studies place the base of the animal family tree in the Tonian, though physical evidence for such early animals is lacking. Sponges, a basal animal group, emerged in the Tonian and survived the glaciations that followed.

prot-095.title: The Arabian-Nubian Shield begins
prot-095.text: The gold of the pharaohs came from rocks made by colliding island chains. From 870 million years ago, island arcs began building the Arabian-Nubian Shield as the Mozambique Ocean closed. Arc collisions and terrane suturing followed at 780 million years ago, with final assembly by 550 million. Gold mined in antiquity in Egypt and Sudan comes almost entirely from these Neoproterozoic rocks.

prot-096.title: The Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event
prot-096.text:
Oxygen's second great rise prepared the world for animals. Called the Second Great Oxidation Event, it raised oxygen in the air and oceans about 850–540 million years ago. Marine rocks of 850–720 million years record a large positive carbon-isotope excursion, a sign that more organic carbon was being buried.

The numbers are dramatic. During 900–815 million years ago, oxygen rose from under 0.1% of present levels to over 13%, and possibly to about 50% in the Cryogenian interglacial. Oxygen rose above 1% of the atmosphere for the first time. Air bubbles trapped in 813-million-year-old rock salt hold 10.9% oxygen.

The change was uneven. It may have been one global event or a series of regional episodes. The deep ocean stayed anoxic and iron-rich as late as 580 million years ago.

Still, the surge drove rapid evolution of multicellular life late in the era. Some authors credit it with letting the oxygen-hungry Ediacaran biota spread. It echoes, on a grander scale, {{ref:prot-006}}.

prot-099.title: The Huainan worms
prot-099.text: Creatures you could see without a microscope were crawling in China 800 million years ago. Near Huainan City, in Anhui, small worm-shaped organisms large enough to see with the naked eye record a transitional stage in evolution, 840–740 million years ago. A similar biota, about 1 billion years old, was found on Russia's Timan Ridge. Both hint that life was moving from microbes toward larger, more complex forms.

prot-100.title: The Adelaide Rift Complex opens
prot-100.text: One Australian basin holds a diary of the late Precambrian. Deposition in the Adelaide Superbasin began just before 830 million years ago, as Laurentia started to rift away from Australia. Its rift troughs and passive-margin basins kept developing until about 550 million years ago. Its rocks record Rodinia's breakup, two Snowball Earth glaciations, the Neoproterozoic oxygenation and the Ediacaran fauna.

prot-102.title: Eukaryotes grow more complex
prot-102.text: Around 800 million years ago, eukaryote fossils became notably more complex and numerous, as sulfide in the oceans fell. By about 750 million years ago, some small algae were mineralized, probably as armor against single-celled eukaryotic predators. The arms race of {{ref:prot-087}} had moved on to hard shells. Yet persistent anoxia and euxinia, oxygen-free and sulfide-rich water, kept overall eukaryotic diversity low through the late Tonian.

prot-104.title: Cyanobacteria take to the open sea
prot-104.text: Tiny floating cells may have helped freeze the planet. Marine planktonic cyanobacteria, drifting in open water, first appeared about 800 million years ago, descended from seafloor and freshwater ancestors, and helped oxygenate the oceans. Their spread is thought to have sped oxygenation and the removal of carbon dioxide, helping explain the severe Cryogenian glaciations. Later, planktonic nitrogen fixers ended a long shortage of ammonium that had held back multicellular life.

prot-105.title: The Pharusian Ocean opens and closes
prot-105.text: As Rodinia tore apart, a new ocean opened along the edge of West Africa. Rifting along the eastern margin of the West African craton opened the Pharusian Ocean about 800 million years ago. It did not last. It began to close about 730 million years ago, as the Tilemsi arc, a chain of volcanoes, was subducted eastward against the Hoggar region.

prot-101.title: The East African Orogeny begins Gondwana
prot-101.text:
Africa, India and Arabia were welded together along a single mountain belt. Gondwana, the great southern continent, began to form about 800–650 million years ago, as India and Madagascar collided with East Africa in the East African Orogeny. It was the main stage in joining East and West Gondwana along the Mozambique Belt, uniting Africa, India and Arabia.

The Arabian-Nubian Shield collided with eastern Africa in the Kenya–Tanzania region. The Mozambique Ocean, between Madagascar–India and the Congo–Tanzania craton, began closing between 700 and 580 million years ago. In one model, arc accretion became a full continental collision when Azania struck the Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block around 640 million years ago.

prot-109.title: The Kaigas glaciation that never was
prot-109.text: Sometimes a glaciation disappears from the textbooks. Conglomerates of the Kaigas Formation on the Kalahari Craton were once read as the mark of a Snowball Earth glaciation about 750 million years ago, before the Sturtian. Then the formation proved to be non-glacial. That leaves no evidence for any Neoproterozoic glaciation before the Sturtian, and the Kaigas glaciation is now rejected.

prot-108.title: Rodinia breaks apart
prot-108.text:
The breakup of a supercontinent may have set off the coldest era in Earth's history. Rifting in Rodinia began as early as 850–800 million years ago, perhaps driven by a superplume. Most agree the breakup proper began about 750 million years ago, with eruptions on most continents.

Rodinia split into Proto-Laurasia, the Congo craton and Proto-Gondwana. New oceans, such as the Adamastor and the proto-Pacific Panthalassa, opened as Mirovia closed. By 750 million years ago Gondwana had rotated away, leaving Laurentia isolated near the equator. When the breakup ended, about 600 million years ago, Baltica was left isolated for some 200 million years.

Between 650 and 550 million years ago the Iapetus Ocean opened, and the Adamastor and Mozambique oceans closed, forming Gondwana, begun in {{ref:prot-101}}.

The consequences reached far beyond geography. The breakup may have triggered the Cryogenian Snowball Earth and the rapid evolution of life that followed.
